utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-96-23/2-PT, the Prosecutor versus Dragan Zelenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We're here today for a hearing under Rule 11 bis. May we have the appearances. Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours; counsel. For the Prosecution, Susan Somers; to my left, Mr. Aleksandar Kontic, legal officer; to my right, extreme right, Ms. Verica Balikic, case manager; assisted by Mr. Greg Bodulovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm attorney-at-law Zoran Jovanovic from Belgrade appearing on behalf of Mr. Dragan Zelenovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And then we have a videolink with Sarajevo. Perhaps I should have first have checked whether the -- I do not receive interpretation at this moment, but -- yes. Could you please introduce yourselves from Sarajevo. That's -- you're representatives of the -- of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your Honours, on behalf of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the delegation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we would like to thank the Referral Chamber for allowing us to participate via videolink. I would now like to introduce to you the members of the delegation. Mr. Emir Neradin, registry office for section 1 and 2 of the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina; Ms. Mechtild Lauth, office of the registrar for department 1 and 2 of the court of Bosnia-Herzegovina; Mr. Philip Alcock from the Prosecutor's office of Bosnia and Herzegovina; Ms. Stephanie Godart of the Prosecutor's office of Bosnia and Herzegovina; and I as head of the delegation, Fatima Basic come from the Ministry of Justice of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Basic, for introducing yourself. Mr. Zelenovic, I had not yet asked you whether you could hear us in a language you understand. Yes, you can?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zelenovic, it maybe clear that additional opportunity will be given to the parties now and to the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina to add whatever they would like to add to their written submissions. You may remain seated. I had in mind to give a short opportunity to the Prosecution to make any further submissions, or to reserve their time, as you have done before, I take it, I remember, Ms. Somers, to say, well, nothing to be added at this moment, but I'd like to have some time at a later stage. I think that altogether some 20 minutes would do. Would you like to add anything at this moment, Ms. Somers, or would you rather reserve your time?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I reserve, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So 20 minutes still available to Ms. Somers. Mr. Jovanovic, is there anything you'd like to add to the submissions you've given already and annexes attached to it, or if you would like to summarise at this moment? You have also -- altogether you have 20 minutes available to -- and if there is any need, if there is a lot of new stuff, then of course you could apply for more time. Anything you'd like to add or to summarise?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Very briefly, given that all of the arguments of the Defence were included in our motion on the 22nd of September, now I would just like to briefly point out some additional issues which were contained in our motion, but I would like to give you additional clarification. Not even in relation to all of the points, just some of the points. I can do it at any time that the Chamber deems convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you want to give any additional clarification, you're invited to do that right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, as I have stated, the arguments of the Defence are contained in our written motion. In a way, the Defence found itself in a situation where we not only challenged the arguments listed by the Prosecution in this referral case, but we also had to challenge some other decisions issued here at ICTY in the case against Stankovic and Jankovic, which is a bit of an awkward situation. I would now like to point out some of the issues that I consider relevant. I am fully aware of the position taken previously by the Referral Chamber about the fact that there exists in Bosnia and Herzegovina a court that can accept the cases referred by the ICTY and that there are no impediments for cases being tried there. What I think needs to be further clarified, and perhaps additional clarification can be given by the representatives of Bosnia and Herzegovina, is the application of the law. In Stankovic and Jankovic cases, the Referral Chamber already took the position considering the law that is to be applied, whether it is going to be the law of the SFRY, which was in force at the time when the crimes were committed, or whether it is going to be the law on criminal law of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was adopted in 2003, the Criminal Code of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And in Annex I of Defence submission, I attached the indictment issued by the prosecutor of the Brcko district dated the 13th of July, 2005, which is to say at the time when the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the war crimes chamber in Sarajevo had already been established and when the new Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina had already been adopted, the code with amendments, particularly those pertaining to Article 4(A) of the Criminal Code. I would like to draw the attention of the Chamber to the fact that this was the case referred by the Prosecution of this Tribunal to the Brcko district. The OTP here did not issue an indictment. However, they completed the entire investigation and referred the case to Bosnia and Herzegovina. The decision of the Prosecution was quite clear. They qualified the crimes in that indictment in the light of the law that was in force at the time when the crimes were committed, which was the Criminal Code of the SFRY. I additionally emphasise that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I beg your pardon for interrupting at this time. But in order -- at this moment so that there is no misunderstanding, it was not a referral by the Office of the Prosecutor. At best, it was a Rules of the Road case. It is not a referred case. So the language I think needs to be clarified considerably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jovanovic, Ms. Somers draws our attention to the fact that it was not a referred case but that it was a case which -- I understand the Rules of the Road with the full consent of the OTP was dealt with by a court in Brcko and not by this Tribunal. They gave the green light to have the case prosecuted over there. Unless you would disagree, you're invited to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Naturally this was a case where the indictment had not yet been issued by this Tribunal. However, the evidence accompanied by the letter of the Prosecutor was sent to Bosnia, to the Brcko district. This was not a case where -- this was not a case of a referral under 11 bis. I fully agree with that. This case pertain to the events in the Luka camp in Brcko. Goran Jelisic was convicted by this Tribunal for the same events, and in this case the same events were included. So as I said, as long as the law of Bosnia and Herzegovina was in force, the Prosecution of Bosnia and Herzegovina qualified these acts, among other things, in Count 4 -- or, rather, in Count 6 of the indictment as rape and other acts based on Article 4. Article 4 speaks of the principle of legality and the principle of lex mitior, that is to say that, namely, the law more beneficial to the accused needs to be applied. The different approach taken by the Prosecution in Bosnia and Herzegovina, even though it concerns in this case the Brcko district, can lead to legal uncertainty; namely, the accused finds himself in a situation where the Referral Chamber submits to the Prosecution and to the Chamber in Bosnia and Herzegovina -- rather, when they allow them to choose which law is going to be applied should the case be referred. So the accused does not know in advance which law is going to be applied. I think that it is necessary to establish very clear criteria --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, this seems to be a big misunderstanding. The only thing this Referral Bench has done in the past is to make sure that whatever law will be applied in accordance with the local legislation, the legislation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, not knowing exactly what case law would develop, that there is nothing in either the old law or in the new law which would result in a situation where the applicable law would not enable to try these cases, without saying anything on which law had to be applied, because it's not within the competence of this Referral Bench to decide for the courts in Bosnia and Herzegovina, how they should interpret their legal system, especially in view of the applicability of law in terms of time. So there's a consistent case law of this Referral Bench which makes abundantly clear, I would say, that this Referral Bench is not saying apply this law or apply that law. We're just having an overview and see that no results could be expected which would be, our law does not provide for the instruments which would allow to punish those who are found guilty of the crimes covered by the indictment as it lies before this Tribunal at this moment. That's the only thing we're doing. So it seems that your argument was based upon a wrong understanding of the task of this Referral Bench. Please proceed and keep this in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. At the outset of my presentation, I said that given the previous rulings of this Chamber has established that there is a firm legal framework in Bosnia-Herzegovina, regardless of which law is going to be applied, be it the one which was in force at the time when the crime was committed or the one that was adopted later, and this is all pursuant Article 4(A). The important distinction that I would like to draw your attention to is the sentence which is provided in the law. At the time, when these crimes were committed, the law which was in force when the crimes were committed stipulated that the maximum sentence was 20 years, whereas the new law specifies that the minimum sentence is 10 years and maximum sentence is 20 to 40 years. I just wanted to reiterate that regardless of the role of the Chamber that you have just explained yourself, at the time when the Chamber rules on whether this case is going to be referred to Sarajevo or not, the accused finds himself in a situation where he doesn't know which law is going to be applied. I think that Bosnia and Herzegovina needs to establish clear criteria as to exactly which law is going to be applied under those circumstances. Naturally, both laws facilitate unhindered proceedings, and naturally there is a possibility that the charges would be dropped and proceedings suspended. Now, as to Bosnia and Herzegovina, I think that they need to clarify the following: Once the case is referred and once --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, are you telling -- at this moment are you saying that Bosnia and Herzegovina should clarify for this Referral Bench, or are you saying Bosnia and Herzegovina should clarify in its future case law, well, whatever you'd like to address? Is it relevant at this moment for our decision, or is it just for future development in the case law of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that in general their position needs to be clarified. As for the jurisprudence of the Referral Bench, it is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, we have some difficulties with the videolink at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems to us that the videolink with Bosnia and Herzegovina has been re-established. Did you miss important parts? Are you long already deprived from what was said in The Hague? Could I ask you, Ms. Basic, to inform me?

utterances.speaker: MS. BASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we didn't miss anything. We heard everything that was said, and we can even reply to the question raised by the Defence. In accordance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would first, as a matter of fact, give an opportunity to Mr. Jovanovic to finish had his argument and then there will be an opportunity to -- to make your observations in relation to that. Mr. Jovanovic, I consulted with my colleagues. The future development of case law in Bosnia-Herzegovina is not something that would be very important, very relevant. We are looking forward to -- to see what happens there, but it's not relevant for our decision at this moment. So you are invited to proceed and to leave this. One question, you said maximum sentence was 20 years under the old law. Isn't it true that death penalty was the maximum sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you're referring to the term of imprisonment that could be imposed. Then that's well understood. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I was referring to the term of imprisonment, because the 20-year imprisonment was in fact a substitute for the death penalty. However, pursuant to further developments, it became impossible to implement the death penalty any longer. I have nothing else to add, Your Honours. I would just like to draw your attention to the fact that it is possible to qualify the act in two different -- significantly different ways given the sentence envisaged for that act, and that it would be beneficial if clear criteria were to be established so that the accused know exactly, even though it's not going to be contained in the decision as you stated, the decision only specifies that it's possible to conduct the proceedings in Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, I think that Bosnia and Herzegovina needs to establish very clear criteria so that the accused knows which law is going to be applied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, now I think for the third time you try to revisit a matter on which I first said that it was based on a misunderstanding, then I said it was irrelevant, and now you try it for the third time, which is -- well, let's say not very intelligent to do. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I just announced that this was it as far as my arguments were concerned in relation to this issue. As for all other directions given to the Defence as to stating our position, it is fully explained in our motion dated the 22nd of September, and I have nothing further to add to it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We've read that carefully. Ms. Basic in Sarajevo, I would like to give you an opportunity to add anything you think of relevance to the submissions, the extensive submissions, including case law, full text case law for us. May I ask you also to keep in mind what I just said to Mr. Jovanovic about the relevance of some of his submissions and that further development of case law in Bosnia and Herzegovina is not within the competence of this Chamber to further elaborate on. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we believe that given the gravity of the crime and the level of criminal responsibility, this case meets the criteria under Rule 11 bis for referral to the BH Prosecutor, especially if we bear in mind the fact that the Stankovic and Jankovic cases were referred and are being successfully tried, all the more reason to back the motion to have this trial, too, referred to Bosnia-Herzegovina. As for the application of law, perhaps my colleague Mr. Neradin can provide an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Neradin, you're invited to deal with the matter. Please keep in mind that of course this Referral Bench has already received a lot of information and has in its decisions I think also already explained what our role in this is. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NERADIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Given the fact that this is not what this hearing is really about, all I can say is that the BH court has already established a body of case law in a number of trials that have been completed so far. The Abduladhim case, the Appeals Chamber of the BH court has passed a judgement in that one. There are three other cases where we have sentences; in the Samardzic, Simsic, and Paunovic cases. The court applied the Bosnia and Herzegovina Criminal Code in these proceedings. These judgements have already been forward and fully explained. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, because we have received the full text of the judgements you're referring to now. I must admit I have not read them in full yet but will do so before a decision will be taken, that we are acquainted with these developments in the case law of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is there anything else, Ms. Basic, you would like, or Mr. Neradin, you'd like to add at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. BASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this point in time, I have nothing to add. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I am moving to you, Ms. Somers. You reserved your time. We're now in the second round, more or less. Would you like to make observations either in addition to what you have put on paper already or in response to what the Defence or the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina has submitted?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just a couple of points and very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: With respect to what has been raised by my learned friend opposite, Mr. Jovanovic, the case, just to set the record straight, that was referred to in Brcko was not an OTP investigation. It was at all times a Bosnian investigation. Strictly rules of road and received a green light in August of 2000 for continued processing in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So that there is no misunderstanding that it was not subject to indictment here as was alleged on page 5, line 16, I believe, in the record. In terms of the level and gravity, which are the principal issues, we stand, of course, on our submissions that this case falls squarely within the contemplated level of the accused, lower to intermediate, and the gravity of offence falls squarely as has been effectively confirmed by this Bench and the Appeals Chamber in the sister case of Jankovic. The fact that those cases are well under way provides a body of law that should be allowed, as I understand it, to be applied to this case should it be referred and allow for a speedy trial in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the state court; that the designation of Bosnia-Herzegovina is correct as we indicated in our submissions. There really should be no issue on that. And that the direct perpetration, 7(1) charges, are the gravamen. There is no 7(3) in this case as both we emphasise and BH. If there is anything we can help the Bench with, please let us know, but I think that we just want to stand on our submissions and correct the record that was made today, as done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jovanovic, is -- do you feel any need at this moment to respond to what Ms. Somers just said?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I believe the matter has been clarified in relation to Annex I. As for the other matter, this is something that has already been raised by the Prosecution and the Defence has already replied to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one question for you, Mr. Jovanovic. You're explaining in your submission that you're concerned about witnesses living in Serbia which under the European Convention on Mutual Assistance in Criminal Matters could not be forced to appear before a court in Sarajevo and might not be inclined to go to Sarajevo. It is not entirely clear to me what your -- what your concern is. Are you afraid to lose them as witnesses at all, or are you concerned about the way in which they'll bring their information, bring their knowledge of the events before the court in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's certainly not the latter. I'm not concerned about that, what the witnesses might possibly say before the court. It's only about the accessibility of witnesses or their desire to respond to a Defence summons to appear in a trial held before a Sarajevo court. There is the ECMACM that exists pursuant to an agreement or a treaty signed between Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia. This sort of assistance would be provided only in cases where witnesses living in Serbia was in a position to testify via videolink at the Sarajevo trial. It is pursuant to that agreement that the Belgrade court would then make sure that all the conditions, technical conditions, were in place for something like that to be done. However, based on a brief preliminary investigation, there are a number of witnesses potentially essential for our case who reside in Belgrade. Any binding summons by a BH court, and this has been explained on a number of occasions because in keeping with the BH Criminal Code it is the duty of a witness to respond to a summons, which is the same as applies in Serbia, and a failure to respond to a summons is liable for penalty. However, a summons cannot be served on citizens of the Republic of Serbia or those residing there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's all clear from your written submissions already, but let me then be more concrete. If they, even after you've explained to them, because you write in your submission they are afraid of being prosecuted, I think the treaty as such, do we agree on that, protects whatever witness who is called to appear on the basis of this convention is -- has a, how do you say, has a safe conduct if he appears? Do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. I may have misunderstood, but it is precisely safe conduct that was discussed when the ruling was made in the Stankovic and Jankovic cases, and doubt was cast on the possibility of their having such a measure implemented. Let's say there is a person who is charged with specific crimes in Bosnia-Herzegovina. If this person resides in Serbia, at the moment this person reaches Bosnian soil this person will be arrested. So safe conduct does not apply in this case. At least that's my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's your position. Although the -- if he is summoned under the convention you just mentioned, he has a safe conduct under that convention. Isn't the convention not quite clear on that? Isn't it true that the European Convention says that someone who is summoned on the basis of this convention and appears before a foreign court could not be arrested, prosecuted, whatever? I mean -- and if you say that's not in the convention -- I haven't got that text here at this moment, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think the position of Bosnia and Herzegovina is that any such person would be arrested, any persons being investigated or under detention measures. The moment they step on Bosnian soil they will be arrested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll ask Bosnia and Herzegovina. But let's just assume that that is then not a way to get these people in before the court in Sarajevo. Isn't it true that under that same convention you could ask a witness to be heard or to be examined in Serbia in the presence of the parties who come from Bosnia and Herzegovina and even could attend the examination of a witness in accordance with that treaty, what they call an examination under letters rogatory?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We're now talking about those witnesses willing to respond to the prompting by the Defence, and then it's down to them to organise a videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, isn't it true that if through letters rogatory a witness would be examined on the territory of Serbia not as part of the trial but perhaps in pre-trial proceedings, that where you couldn't force a witness to come from Serbia to Sarajevo, that you could, however, force a witness to appear before in his local court and be examined there so that at least the transcripts or the report of that testimony or -- perhaps I shouldn't call it testimony, but that statement can then be used abroad in Sarajevo? And isn't it true that under those circumstances it depends on Serbian law that the situation were exactly the same if someone if -- if someone was summoned before a Serbian court and is therefore under an obligation to appear?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you're entirely right. My interpretation is much the same as in Bosnia-Herzegovina there is the obligation of a witness to attend a Serbian court for proceedings being held before a Serbian court. The Law on Criminal Procedure applies to proceedings before Serbian courts. Therefore, if there's a summons by a BH court and the person receiving the summons lives, resides in Serbia, there is no obligation whatsoever to appear and to respond to the summons, unlike a situation with a tribunal which has the power to issue a binding summons. So a Bosnian court has no power to issue any form of binding summons to anyone, resident or citizen of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems, Mr. Jovanovic, we still do not yet understand each other. Let me try to be clearer. If -- and we are still talking about the European Convention on Mutual Assistance in Criminal Matters. If a court in Bosnia and Herzegovina would like to receive the information available to a witness who lives in Serbia and who is unwilling to come to Bosnia and Herzegovina, couldn't they then ask the Serbian authorities to examine that witness in Serbia before a Serbian judge, add to that request that the parties in the Bosnia and Herzegovina case could attend that examination of the witness? Would the witness under those circumstances not be under an obligation to appear before the Serbian court where he gives testimony which will then be relayed on paper to the court in Bosnia and Herzegovina? That's the situation I'm talking about. Is that a possibility, in your view; and would he be under an obligation then to appear before his Serbian court?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my interpretation of the agreement is that this means assistance. A court in Serbia can and indeed must, within the terms of this agreement, make sure that a witness is heard, but I don't think this is binding for any citizen of Serbia to appear and testify before a Sarajevo court. So although this may be done before a court in Belgrade, this is still a trial that is held before a court in Bosnia and Herzegovina. In that sense, there is nothing binding and no obligation. Perhaps we could imagine a similar situation. Say the OTP are summoning a person in Serbia for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, have you any case law to rely upon, any practice which would support your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is not an example from the case law. I am in touch with the justice ministry of the Republic of Serbia, their legal assistance department, and they told me about this position that I'm informing you about now. There have been videolinks between the Belgrade court and the Sarajevo court, and this seems to work very well, but that still doesn't mean that a witness can be subpoenaed to appear at a Sarajevo court in any way. My grievance was therefore related to the impossibility to ensure the presence of a witness before the court in Sarajevo. I was just telling you that this Tribunal has the power to order a witness to appear, irrespective of the witness's place of residence or nationality. This Tribunal has the power to subpoena a witness and to issue binding orders to the witness's country, whereas the BH court does not have the same powers, and I don't think an agreement has been signed that might further this process and cooperation in legal matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for these answers, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'd like to give an opportunity to you, Ms. Basic, to respond to what was said by Mr. Jovanovic. He suggested that if through the channels of the European Convention on Mutual Assistance in criminal cases, if someone would be summoned living in Serbia that that witness would not enjoy a safe conduct as provided for in that convention. Could you please respond to that, because it was not totally clear to me on what basis Mr. Jovanovic took that position.

utterances.speaker: MS. BASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I would like to pass the floor to Mr. Neradin for this issue. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Neradin, you may understand that I was specifically referring to -- I think it's Article 12 of that -- of that convention. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NERADIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you've already stated, Bosnia-Herzegovina is a signatory to the ECMACM. It is pursuant to Article 12 of that convention there is guarantee of immunity to all witnesses summoned before this court that are nationals of a different country. Bosnia and Herzegovina has ratified a contract with Serbia and Montenegro in legal assistance in criminal and civil matters. On the 2nd of June, 2005, Article 14 guaranteed the same sort of immunity to those subject to criminal prosecution. These witnesses are free to leave within 15 days after their presence is no longer legally required. As for forcing a witness or subpoenaing a witness from Serbia, generally speaking, if there is a witness who refuses to appear, there is the possibility of using the instrument of legal assistance and legal cooperation, be it by videolink, as counsel has mentioned, or by taking a deposition from a witness pursuant to all these international agreements that are after all binding for Bosnia and Herzegovina. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your clarification, Mr. Neradin. I have at this moment no further question. I'm looking to my colleagues. They have no further questions. Then I would give a brief opportunity to the parties, if there is need to add anything which has been said, you have an opportunity to do that now. Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can see nothing further that would need to be added.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Basic, is there anything you'd like to add from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MS. BASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, there is nothing we would like to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Finally, Mr. Zelenovic, you have been here listening to argument which is of a rather high technical nature, legally technical nature. I can imagine that there is nothing you would like to add to that, but if there's anything at this moment you'd like to say, and you are aware we -- I mean, we are dealing with these legal technical matters because it is of course for you not a legal technical matter, but it's what will happen to you, but if you'd like to add anything, you may do so.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone was not on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you switch on your microphone if you say something. Mr. Zelenovic, the interpreters couldn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zelenovic. Please be seated. The Chamber will consider everything that has been submitted and will give its decision in due course, or if it feels that it's not able yet, to return to the parties. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: at 4.53 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Rule 11 bis Hearing adjourned
